transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I’m here because this has been going on for months, and I feel like nobody is really listening to me. It’s about my husband’s family. They’ve been quietly interfering with our money and with my reputation, our good name, you know? Not in some obvious way where you can point to one big thing, but in these little things that keep happening.

Like at work, I’m a billing clerk, so I notice numbers. I notice when something is off. Little billing errors come up, things that make me look careless, and people act like it’s just a mistake or they pull up records and say, “See, this doesn’t prove anything,” but I know how this connects. And then at church someone will suddenly be strange with me, like they’ve heard something or been told something, and I can feel the shift. It’s not random.

I’ve tried to explain it, but people keep focusing on whether I can show one document that says his family did it. That’s not how they work. It’s quiet. It’s spread out. But I know it ties back to them, and I need someone to understand that instead of just brushing me off.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, not voices like you’re describing, like someone talking when nobody’s there. I hear people talk at work or at church, of course, and sometimes I wonder what they’ve been told, because the way they lower their voices or stop when I come near, it feels like there’s something behind it. But I wouldn’t say I’m hearing voices out of nowhere.

It’s more… I notice how people act, what changes, the little comments, the timing of things. That’s different from hearing a voice in an empty room. I know the difference.
Do you believe your husband’s family has any special way of controlling events around you that other people would say is impossible?

I don’t mean like… magic or something like that, if that’s what you’re asking. I’m not saying they have some impossible power. It’s more that they know how to work quietly, through people, through little situations, so by the time something happens it looks like nothing.

Like with the money and the billing things at work — I’m a billing clerk, I know how records look when they’re right and when something is off. And when these little errors pop up, not huge enough for someone to say, “Here, this proves it,” but just enough to make me look careless, it’s hard for me to believe that’s all accidental. Then the same kind of thing happens socially, like at church, where someone who was perfectly normal with me suddenly acts cold or careful around me. People say, “Well, maybe they were just having a bad day,” but when it keeps lining up, you start to see the pattern.

So no, not controlling events in an impossible way. But influencing things, yes. Quietly. In ways other people don’t want to take seriously because they can’t put one piece of paper in front of me and say, “This is the proof.” But I know it ties back to my husband’s family. I’ve been living with it for months.
Have you had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or irritable for days at a time?

I’m not sure I’d call it “high.” I mean, I get upset, yes, especially when I feel like people are acting as if I’m making things up or when something happens and everyone wants to pretend it’s just a coincidence. That can make me feel keyed up, and I’ll think about it a lot because I’m trying to sort out what happened and why.

But if you mean like being unusually energized for days, like not myself, or feeling on top of the world or something… I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed that in that way. Irritable, maybe, but I think anyone would be irritable if they were dealing with this and nobody was taking it seriously. So I don’t know if that counts as what you’re asking.
Because this started, has your ability to do your job gone downhill?

Not really downhill in the sense of, like, I haven’t been fired or written up or anything like that. I’m still going in, doing the billing work, keeping up with my regular responsibilities. I mean, I may double-check things more than I used to, because I don’t want anyone saying I made a mistake when I didn’t, but I still get the work done.

Where it’s affected things more is outside of that, honestly. My husband and I have argued more because he thinks I should just let it go, or he acts like I’m making something out of nothing, and that’s frustrating. And at church there have been some uncomfortable moments, because people seem to want me to stop bringing it up or pretend everything is fine. So socially, yes, it’s made things awkward. At home, yes, more tension. But my job itself — I’m still functioning, I’m still taking care of what I’m supposed to take care of.
About how long have you been dealing with this situation with your husband’s family?

It’s been about nine months now, I’d say. It really started after that trouble with my husband’s family over money, and then the expectations around the holidays — who was supposed to do what, pay for what, show up where, all of that. At first I thought it was just family tension, you know, something that would blow over, but it didn’t.

So… yes, about nine months. Long enough that it’s not just one misunderstanding or one bad week. It’s been going on long enough that I can look back and see when things shifted.
Have you had the feeling that people can read your thoughts?

No, I don’t think they’re reading my thoughts exactly. It’s not like I believe someone can hear words in my head or anything like that.

What I do think is that people are picking up things or being told things somehow, because there are these little things that keep happening. Like with my husband’s family — for months I’ve been trying to explain that they’re quietly interfering with our money and how people see us. Then a billing error shows up at work, or someone at church suddenly acts strange toward me, like they’ve heard something or they’re looking at me differently, and everyone wants to say it’s unrelated. But it doesn’t feel unrelated to me.

So, no, not reading my thoughts. It’s more like they know things or are spreading things, and no matter what records people pull up, I can see how it ties back to them.
Have you ever felt that something outside you was putting thoughts into your mind?

No, not like that. I don’t feel like someone is putting thoughts into my head or controlling what I think. My thoughts feel like my own.

What I keep trying to explain is different. It’s that for months now, I’ve been seeing how my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. It’s not some random idea that just appeared in my head from outside — it’s from things that keep happening. Like little billing errors showing up at work, or someone at church suddenly acting funny toward me, like they’ve heard something about me or they’re treating me differently. And then people want to pull up records or explain it away like it’s all separate, but I know it ties back to them.

So no, I wouldn’t say thoughts are being put into my mind. It’s more that I can see what’s going on, and it’s frustrating because other people keep acting like I’m the only one noticing it.
When you talk, do people ever tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that doesn’t make sense to them?

I don’t think so… I mean, not in the sense that people tell me I’m not making sense. I can be long-winded, I know that. My husband has said I explain things with too much detail, and sometimes people want me to get to the point faster, especially at work when everyone’s busy and they just want the short version.

But I don’t think people say I jump around in a way that doesn’t make sense. I may go back and fill in details because I feel like if I leave something out, then the whole thing gets misunderstood. So I’ll start with one part and then remember another part that matters, and I’ll circle back. To me it all connects, but I know it can probably sound like I’m giving more than they asked for.

So… hard to follow, maybe because I talk too much sometimes. But not because my words don’t make sense, at least not that anyone has really told me.
Have you ever felt that other people were controlling your actions?

No, I don’t think anyone is controlling my actions. I mean, I make my own decisions, I go to work, I do what I need to do, and I don’t feel like someone is moving me around or making me say or do things.

Sometimes I might feel pressured by people, or like other people’s behavior affects what I have to do next — like if someone creates a problem, then I have to respond to it — but that’s not the same as them controlling my body or my actions. I know when I choose to do something. So no, I wouldn’t describe it that way.
If someone shows you evidence that your husband’s family was not involved in one of these incidents, are you able to accept that for that incident?

Well… I can look at whatever someone wants to show me, and I’m not saying every single paper in front of me is fake or anything like that. If there’s a record that says one particular charge was entered by this person or that person, I can understand what the record says for that one little piece.

But what frustrates me is people act like showing me one record should make me ignore the whole pattern. These things have been happening for months — little billing errors showing up at work, people suddenly acting strange toward me at church, the way our money and our reputation seem to keep getting touched in these quiet ways. So if someone says, “Here, this proves they weren’t involved in this one incident,” I might say, fine, maybe not directly on that one paper or in that one step. But that doesn’t mean they weren’t behind it somehow, or that it doesn’t still tie back to them.

That’s the part people don’t seem to understand. They want to separate everything out like it’s all random, but when you’re the one living it, you see how it connects. So I can accept a detail, maybe, but I don’t just drop the whole thing because someone pulls up a record.
Have you lost interest in being around other people or in activities you used to enjoy?

No, not exactly. I mean, I still do things. I get up and go to work, and I handle my billing clerk duties. I may be tired of dealing with certain people, but I’m not just sitting at home doing nothing. I keep the house going, I take care of what needs taking care of.

And I still like my own things, like gardening. That’s actually calming for me, because plants don’t twist things around, you know? And painting, too — when I have the time and the right frame of mind, I still enjoy that. So I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in everything or stopped wanting to do anything.

Where it gets difficult is more when I’m around people and I try to warn them about what my in-laws are doing. That’s when it changes. People get uncomfortable, or they act like I’m being dramatic, and then it makes me not want to keep explaining myself over and over. So it’s not that I don’t care about people or activities anymore. It’s more that some situations become hard because of how people react when I bring up what’s been going on.
Before these past nine months, have you generally tended to mistrust other people and suspect that they might be trying to harm or deceive you?

No, I really don’t think I was always like this. I mean, I’ve never been stupid about people — if someone seems dishonest, I notice it — but I wasn’t going around suspecting everybody or thinking people were out to get me.

This really started about nine months ago, after all that trouble with my husband’s family over money and the holiday expectations. That’s when things changed. Before that, I could get annoyed with people like anyone else, but I didn’t have this constant feeling that I had to watch what they were doing or figure out what was behind things. It’s been since that situation with them that I started seeing how these things were connecting.
Have you felt emotionally flat or unable to show much feeling lately?

Emotionally flat? I don’t know that I’d put it that way. I still feel things, definitely. I get upset, I get frustrated, I can laugh if something is actually funny, and I still care about what’s happening around me.

Maybe I don’t always show everything the way people expect me to. Sometimes if I’m worn out or if I feel like someone is judging me, I might get quieter, but that’s not the same as not feeling anything. Inside I’m usually feeling plenty. So no, I haven’t really noticed being unable to show feeling. I may be guarded at times, but not flat.
Did this start suddenly over a few days?

No, I wouldn’t say it was suddenly over just a few days. It’s been going on for about nine months now, really since that whole trouble started with my husband’s family — the money issues and all the holiday expectations, all of that.

It wasn’t like I woke up one morning and everything was different. It built from there, but that’s when I’d say it started, around nine months ago.

No, I don’t think anyone is controlling my actions. I mean, I make my own decisions, I go to work, I do what I need to do, and I don’t feel like someone is moving me around or making me say or do things.

Sometimes I might feel pressured by people, or like other people’s behavior affects what I have to do next — like if someone creates a problem, then I have to respond to it — but that’s not the same as them controlling my body or my actions. I know when I choose to do something. So no, I wouldn’t describe it that way.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the suspicious belief is held with delusional conviction despite contrary evidence, helping distinguish a persistent delusional disorder from paranoid personality traits.
doctor.question: If someone shows you evidence that your husband’s family was not involved in one of these incidents, are you able to accept that for that incident?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for months now I’ve been trying to get people to understand that my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money and our good name, like when little billing errors show up at work or someone at church suddenly acts funny toward me, and no matter what records anyone pulls up I know it ties back to them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief about the husband’s family changes when presented with contradictory evidence, which directly assesses fixed delusional beliefs.

patient.answer:
Well… I can look at whatever someone wants to show me, and I’m not saying every single paper in front of me is fake or anything like that. If there’s a record that says one particular charge was entered by this person or that person, I can understand what the record says for that one little piece.

But what frustrates me is people act like showing me one record should make me ignore the whole pattern. These things have been happening for months — little billing errors showing up at work, people suddenly acting strange toward me at church, the way our money and our reputation seem to keep getting touched in these quiet ways. So if someone says, “Here, this proves they weren’t involved in this one incident,” I might say, fine, maybe not directly on that one paper or in that one step. But that doesn’t mean they weren’t behind it somehow, or that it doesn’t still tie back to them.

That’s the part people don’t seem to understand. They want to separate everything out like it’s all random, but when you’re the one living it, you see how it connects. So I can accept a detail, maybe, but I don’t just drop the whole thing because someone pulls up a record.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed non-bizarre delusion with otherwise preserved functioning (delusional disorder, persecutory type) from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis by testing for prominent negative symptoms.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in being around other people or in activities you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still get up for work, handle my billing clerk duties, keep the house going, and spend time gardening or painting; the main trouble comes up when I try to warn people about what my in-laws are doing.
target_item.reason: The question asks about loss of interest in socializing or activities, which is most directly addressed by the profile item describing preserved functioning and continued activities like gardening and painting.

patient.answer:
No, not exactly. I mean, I still do things. I get up and go to work, and I handle my billing clerk duties. I may be tired of dealing with certain people, but I’m not just sitting at home doing nothing. I keep the house going, I take care of what needs taking care of.

And I still like my own things, like gardening. That’s actually calming for me, because plants don’t twist things around, you know? And painting, too — when I have the time and the right frame of mind, I still enjoy that. So I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in everything or stopped wanting to do anything.

Where it gets difficult is more when I’m around people and I try to warn them about what my in-laws are doing. That’s when it changes. People get uncomfortable, or they act like I’m being dramatic, and then it makes me not want to keep explaining myself over and over. So it’s not that I don’t care about people or activities anymore. It’s more that some situations become hard because of how people react when I bring up what’s been going on.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a premorbid pattern of pervasive suspiciousness and mistrust consistent with paranoid personality disorder rather than a circumscribed delusional disorder or schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis.
doctor.question: Before these past nine months, have you generally tended to mistrust other people and suspect that they might be trying to harm or deceive you?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, ever since the trouble with my husband’s family over money and holiday expectations.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the suspiciousness existed before the current nine-month period, which is most directly related to the duration/onset of the delusional concerns.

patient.answer:
No, I really don’t think I was always like this. I mean, I’ve never been stupid about people — if someone seems dishonest, I notice it — but I wasn’t going around suspecting everybody or thinking people were out to get me.

This really started about nine months ago, after all that trouble with my husband’s family over money and the holiday expectations. That’s when things changed. Before that, I could get annoyed with people like anyone else, but I didn’t have this constant feeling that I had to watch what they were doing or figure out what was behind things. It’s been since that situation with them that I started seeing how these things were connecting.

inference.note: Removed F60.0 because longstanding paranoid personality traits were denied prior to the past 9 months. Removed F31.2 because there is no clear manic syndrome. Persistent, systematized persecutory delusions with relatively preserved functioning most strongly support F22; F23 and F20.0 remain as less likely psychotic differentials.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any persistent negative symptoms, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder or acute/transient psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you felt emotionally flat or unable to show much feeling lately?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about emotional flatness or reduced emotional expression, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Emotionally flat? I don’t know that I’d put it that way. I still feel things, definitely. I get upset, I get frustrated, I can laugh if something is actually funny, and I still care about what’s happening around me.

Maybe I don’t always show everything the way people expect me to. Sometimes if I’m worn out or if I feel like someone is judging me, I might get quieter, but that’s not the same as not feeling anything. Inside I’m usually feeling plenty. So no, I haven’t really noticed being unable to show feeling. I may be guarded at times, but not flat.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms had an abrupt onset, which would help distinguish acute/transient psychotic disorder (F23) from persistent delusional disorder (F22) and paranoid schizophrenia (F20.0).
doctor.question: Did this start suddenly over a few days?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, ever since the trouble with my husband’s family over money and holiday expectations.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the timing and onset of the symptoms, which is most directly covered by the duration item.

patient.answer:
No, I wouldn’t say it was suddenly over just a few days. It’s been going on for about nine months now, really since that whole trouble started with my husband’s family — the money issues and all the holiday expectations, all of that.

It wasn’t like I woke up one morning and everything was different. It built from there, but that’s when I’d say it started, around nine months ago.

inference.note: Nine-month fixed persecutory delusion with otherwise preserved functioning; no hallucinations, thought insertion/broadcast/control, disorganization, negative symptoms, mania, or longstanding paranoid personality traits. Duration and gradual course rule out F23; lack of schizophrenia-defining symptoms argues against F20.0.

opening_question.intent: Elicit the patient's chief concern in their own words to begin narrowing the diagnosis
opening_question.question: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory belief lasting about 9 months that her husband's family is quietly interfering with finances and reputation. She maintains this belief despite contrary evidence, while denying hallucinations, thought insertion, thought broadcasting, passivity, disorganized speech, negative symptoms, and manic symptoms. Functioning is largely preserved except for marital and social strain. This pattern is most consistent with persistent delusional disorder, persecutory type.
